Question three. What's the difference between L one and L two regularization? Both add a penalty on the size of the coefficients. L two, called ridge, penalizes their squares. L one, called lasso, penalizes their absolute values. Here are ten measurements from a diabetes study. Raise the penalty, and ridge shrinks all ten together, keeping every one. Lasso drives them to exactly zero, one at a time. At this strength, it keeps seven. That's feature selection. Question four. What is elastic net? A mix of the two penalties. Two cholesterol measures here move together, with a correlation of point nine. Lasso keeps one and drops the other. Elastic net keeps both, which makes it steadier when features are correlated. So how far can you trust a validation score?

Question five. What is cross-validation, and why use it? Split this tumor data into training and test sets two hundred different ways, and the same model scores anywhere from ninety-four point seven percent to a hundred. One split is one draw from that range. K-fold cross-validation cuts the rows into five folds, trains on four, and scores the fifth, five times over, so every row is scored once. Here, the mean is ninety-seven point nine, give or take one point four. For time series, keep the order: validate only on data that comes after the training data. Question six. What's the discipline behind training, validation and test sets? Fit on the training set. Tune and choose on the validation set, or with cross-validation. Touch the test set once, at the end, to report. Every choice made by looking at the test score makes that score flatter you. And when a model disappoints, a picture tells you what to try next.
